section_1.title: Prerequisites: The Vector Space Concept
section_1.content: Briefly define how computers represent words as vectors (lists of numbers). Use a 2D coordinate system to visualize that words with similar meanings (e.g., 'King' and 'Queen') occupy nearby positions in space.
section_1.example: Imagine a 2D map: 'Dog' and 'Puppy' are clustered in the bottom-left corner, while 'Car' and 'Truck' are in the top-right.

section_2.title: The Core Problem: Contextual Ambiguity
section_2.content: Explain that traditional models read sequentially and often 'forget' the beginning of a sentence. Introduce the concept of 'Attention'—allowing the model to look at all parts of a sequence simultaneously.
section_2.example: In the sentence 'The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired', the word 'it' refers to the animal. A Transformer links 'it' directly to 'animal' using an attention bridge.

section_3.title: The Transformer: The 'Attention' Mechanism
section_3.content: Visualize the 'Self-Attention' mechanism as a spotlight. For every word in a sentence, the model assigns a weight to every other word, indicating how much 'focus' it should have. Mathematically, this is the Softmax of the dot product of Query and Key vectors.
section_3.example: Represent this as an animation where each word (e.g., 'Bank') emits rays to other words; if the context is 'river', the ray to 'water' glows bright, changing the word's meaning.

section_4.title: Scaling Up: Why 'Large' Matters
section_4.content: Explain that LLMs are simply Transformers scaled to billions of parameters and trained on massive datasets. The more parameters, the more nuanced the internal 'map' of human language becomes.
section_4.example: Compare a 'Tiny' model to a toddler with a small vocabulary, and an 'LLM' to a librarian who has read every book in the world, allowing for complex reasoning.

section_5.title: Summary & Application
section_5.content: Conclude by showing how these components—Vector representation, Multi-head Attention, and Massive scale—combine to generate human-like text.
section_5.example: Show a robot character 'generating' a poem by traversing its vector space, picking the next most likely word based on the weighted 'attention' it paid to the user's prompt.
